Ni-Catalyzed Synthesis of Multisubstituted Allenes via
Reductive Cross-Coupling of Propargylic Acetates with
Chlorohydrosilanes
Xiaohui Yan<sup>[a]</sup> and Hong Deng*<sup>[a]</sup>
This paper introduces an innovative strategy for the synthesis of
multisubstituted allenes via nickel-catalyzed reductive cross-
coupling reactions. The approach utilizes propargyl acetates
and chlorosilanes to produce a variety of silyl-substituted
allenes. The reaction conditions are notably mild, and the
process is characterized by high chemo- and regioselectivity, as

Introduction
Allenes are pivotal molecular structures that are integral to a
myriad of natural products and bioactive pharmaceuticals.<sup>[1]</sup>
Their versatile reactivity positions allenes as indispensable
components in the synthesis of natural products and pharma-
ceutical compounds.<sup>[2]</sup> As a result, allenes are unmatched in the
realm of organic synthesis, making their synthesis a topic of
considerable interest among chemists. The broad applicability
of allenes is due to their unique chemical structure, which is
crucial in organic synthesis, natural product research, pharma-
ceutical development, and the creation of functional materials.<sup>[3]</sup>
Currently, various strategies for the synthesis of allenes have
been established,<sup>[4]</sup> including the transition metal-catalyzed
nucleophilic substitution reactions of propargyl compounds
containing leaving groups (Scheme 1a).<sup>[5]</sup> These reactions can
utilize a range of reactive groups such as acetates, methanesul-
fonates, carbonates, and halogens, as leaving groups. Grignard
reagents, organoborons, terminal alkynes, hydrosilanes, and
other nucleophilic reagents have been demonstrated to be
effective coupling partners.<sup>[6]</sup> The recent progress in nickel-
catalyzed reductive cross-coupling process has introduced a
novel approach to the synthesis of allenes. Wang’s group has
successfully synthesized multisubstituted allenes using propar-
gylic carbonates and alkyl iodides in a nickel-catalyzed reduc-
tive cross-coupling process (Scheme 1b).<sup>[7]</sup>
Organosilanes, with their extensive applications in pharma-
ceuticals, pesticides, and functional materials, have sparked
significant research interest.<sup>[8]</sup> Traditional methods for construct-
can be readily extended to the use of chlorogermane and
chlorostannane, facilitating the synthesis of germanium or
stannium-substituted allenes. This research not only offers a
valuable strategy for the preparation of multisubstituted allenes
but also significantly broadens the synthetic repertoire for the
construction of highly functionalized molecules.

Moreover, the versatile reaction conditions can be adapted for
the synthesis of alkylgermane-substituted allenes and alkyltin-
substituted allenes. Recently, Li’s group reported instances of
nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling for the synthesis of
silylenes.<sup>[12]</sup> Additionally, there have been reports on the
synthesis of silylenes through electroreductive cross-cou-
pling.<sup>[9f],[9i]</sup> However, existing examples have focused solely on
radicals, whereas our reaction opens up new possibilities by
achieving reductive cross-coupling with chlorohydrosilanes,
allowing for a wider range of substrate derivatisation in later

Reducing the amount of chloromethylphenylsilane 2 a to
equimolar proportions resulted in a 53% yield decrease
(entry 7). Additionally, abbreviating the reaction time to
15 hours was detrimental, as the starting material was not
completely consumed, leading to a lower yield (entry 8). More-
over, conducting the reaction at room temperature significantly
impaired the yield of product 3 aa (entry 9). It is crucial to
emphasize that both the Ni catalyst and the reducing agent Mn
are indispensable for the reaction; without their presence, the
product 3aa cannot be obtained (entry 10).
Having optimized the reaction conditions for the reductive
coupling reaction to synthesize silyl-substituted allenes, we
proceeded to explore the versatility of this method using a
variety of propargyl
acetates with different structural and functional groups
(Scheme 2). Reassuringly, > arylpropargyl acetates with para-
alkyl substituents were found to be highly amenable to the
reaction, yielding the corresponding allene products (3ba-3ea)
with 60–90 % yields. The reaction was also efficient with
arylpropargyl acetates bearing phenyl substituents, such as 1 f,
which produced the product 3 fa in good yields. Furthermore,
arylpropargyl acetates containing electron-donating methoxyl
groups were compatible with the C�Si reductive cross-coupling,
affording the target molecule 3 ga in an 84 % yield. Substrates
with electron-withdrawing groups like F, Cl, CF3, and OCF3 also
performed well, yielding products 3 ha-3ka in the range of
67 %-83% yields. Furthermore, the reaction demonstrated
broad compatibility with a range of substrates, including those
featuring 1,3-benzodioxole, 1-naphthalene, thiophene, and m-
Me groups. These diverse substrates were successfully trans-
formed into their respective allene products (3la–3 oa) with
yields ranging from 54 % to 88 %. Notably, substrates 1 q and
1 r, featuring 3,5-dimethyl and o-methoxy substitutions, respec-
tively, successfully yielded their corresponding products. It is
significant to highlight that this reaction is not limited to aryl-
substituted substrates, as alkyl-substituted substrates, including
cycloalkanes and chain alkanes (1 s-u), were also found to be
compatible. These alkyl-substituted substrates enabled the
efficient synthesis of the corresponding allenes with high yields.
This finding was further supported by the successful
compatibility of arylpropargyl acetate substrates with a
cycloalkane skeleton. We tested cyclopentane, cyclohexane, and
cycloheptane derivatives, all of which smoothly underwent the
reaction to yield the desired products 3 va–3xa. Additionally,
when the substrate was switched to two ethyl-substituted
phenylpropargyl acetates, the product 3 ya was obtained in a
71 % yield. Lastly, we investigated unsymmetrical substrates
( 1 \pmb { \mathrm { a } } ^ { \prime } \mathbf { - } \pmb { \mathrm { f } } ^ { \prime } )
and achieved favorable results under the established
reaction conditions.

Following an in-depth investigation into the versatility of
propargyl acetate substrates in nickel-catalyzed reductive cross-
coupling reactions, we redirected our focus to assess the
suitability of a variety of chlorosilanes as potential coupling
partners in this reaction (Scheme 3). Our studies revealed that
not only hydrochlorosilanes but also other chlorosilanes are
amenable to this reaction. For example, vinyl dimethyl chlor-
osilane 2 b was successfully reacted to yield allene products.
Additionally, trimethylchlorosilane, a staple reagent in organic
synthesis, proved to be compatible with the reaction, leading to
the synthesis of the trimethylsilyl-substituted allene 3 ac.
Triethylchlorosilane also yielded similar results, and we further
explored the reaction’s tolerance to dimethylisopropylchlorosi-
lane, which afforded the target molecule 3 ae in moderate
yields. We then extended our investigation to the compatibility
of vinyl dimethyl chlorosilane with a range of propargyl
acetates. Moreover, the reaction’s compatibility with unsym-
metrical substrates was also scrutinized. It was observed that
phenylpropargyl acetate substrates, which contain a chain
methyl ester, are highly compatible with the reaction, yielding
the desired product 3e’b. Similarly, propargyl acetate substrates
with long alkyl chain substitutions also produced the product
3 zb in good yields. For instance, the reaction of phenylproparg-
yl acetates with both methyl and isobutyl substitutions with
vinyl dimethylchlorosilane and trimethylchlorosilane was suc-
cessful, resulting in the formation of silyl-substituted allenes
(3b’b–3b’c). It is noteworthy that phenylpropargyl acetate
substrates with a single methyl substitution also performed well
under the reaction conditions described, yielding satisfactory
amounts of the desired product

After delving into the nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling of
propargyl acetates with chlorosilanes for the synthesis of
allenes, we then set our sights on exploring the potential for
coupling reactions with other elements from Group 14 of the
periodic table (Scheme 4). Our ambition was to synthesize
germanium-substituted allenes, and we achieved this by
reductively coupling trimethylgermanium chloride with prop-
argyl acetate under standard conditions. The resulting product,

substituted allenes, albeit with a relatively modest yield. We
also contemplated whether the reductive coupling using
trimethyltin chloride could be accomplished under the current
reaction conditions. Fortunately, the alkyltin-substituted allene
compound 3 ag was successfully synthesized within our reac-
tion system, overcoming the synthetic challenges associated
with conventional methods. The efficient and effective synthesis
of multisubstituted allenes was thus realized through the
successful synthesis of alkylgermanium- and alkyltin-substituted
allenes.

3aa in 68 % yield under standard reaction conditions (Sche-
me 5a). Following this, we initiated derivatisation studies on the
silyl-substituted allene 3 aa, as depicted in Scheme 5b. The
synthesis of tetrasubstituted vinyl product 4 was successfully
achieved by treating the tetrasubstituted allene 3 aa with
phenylselenium chloride. The reaction conditions were simple

mechanism, we conducted several experiments. To determine if

Conclusions
In conclusion, this study presents an innovative approach for
the synthesis of silyl-substituted allenes through nickel-cata-
lyzed reductive cross-coupling reactions between propargylic
acetates and chlorohydrosilanes. This reaction system demon-
strates versatility by accommodating a variety of chlorohydrosi-
lanes and chlorosilanes, while showing exceptional tolerance
towards different functional groups. The simplicity and mild
conditions of this method make it a convenient pathway to
access a diverse range of silyl-substituted allene compounds.
Moreover, the broad applicability of this reaction strategy
extends to chlorogermananes and chlorostannanes, thereby
broadening the scope of possible reactions. Currently, our
research efforts are directed towards exploring the enantiose-
lective synthesis potential of this reaction, which could further
enhance its synthetic utility and applicability in the field of
organic chemistry.

Typical Procedure for the Synthesis of Multisubstituted
Allenes Compounds (3)
Procedure: The procedure was conducted in an nitrogen-filled
glove box. To a reaction tube equipped with a magnetic stir bar
was charged with Ni(PCy ) Cl (13.8 mg, 0.02 mmol), 3,4,7,8-
Me Phen (9.4 mg, 0.04 mmol), Mn (33.0 mg, 0.6 mmol), propargyl
ester 1 (0.2 mmol), Chlorosilanes 2 (0.6 mmol), and DMF (1.5 mL).
The reaction tube was sealed and removed from the glove box. The
reaction mixture was stirred at 0 °C for 24 h. The reaction was
quenched with water (2.0 mL) and extracted with ethyl acetate (3
�15.0 mL). The combined organic layers was washed with water (2
�15.0 mL), brine (15.0 mL), dried over anhydrous Na SO , and
concentrated under reduced pressure. The residue was purified by
flash chromatography on silica gel (PE/EA, from 200 : 1 to 50 :1) to
afford the desired product 3.
